footnote.text: So it becomes about the funding.

brief.head: The tank and the robot
brief.text: Early engines won by brute force. Kasparov, Amit Varma said, likened it to wanting a robot to climb Everest and getting a tank that rolled up. {052-C03}

brief.head: A civilised game
brief.text: Chess has an open category, not a men’s one, Amit Varma said. Unlike poker’s hostile tables, it is “a beautiful civilized world with really decent people”. {052-C16}

brief.head: A champion in a pocket
brief.text: Every mobile phone can now beat the world champion, a friend told Ajay Shah. What saddens him is how little people do with this miracle. {052-S15}

brief.head: Real but overblown
brief.text: Cheating is an enormous threat but an overblown one, Amit Varma said. Top events use metal detectors, closed halls and a 20-minute broadcast delay. {052-S14}

brief.head: Number one, briefly
brief.text: Amit Varma plays variants such as Atomic Chess and Fog of War, where heuristics fail. In a couple he was briefly number one on chess.com. {052-S21}

thought.text: Every game of chess is like a conversation.
thought.who: Amit Varma, after Levon Aronian smiled through a lost game

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the game they both love
lead.head: Board games and power games
body: Amit Varma played serious chess in college until he was nineteen. Then he retired, he said, when he realised that he could not be an Anand: in the early 1990s, below Anand’s level, you could not make a living from the game. {052-S01}
He never stopped following it. Chess is one of the three sports he tracks most closely, and in this episode, which Ajay Shah introduced as the fourth of their “beer sessions”, Varma told its story.

The occasion was D Gukesh reaching the world championship match. For many Indians that is a nationalistic thing, Varma said, and a good reason to celebrate. He wanted to add the history and the context.
## The price of a title

For decades, the title belonged partly to whoever could pay for it. After Wilhelm Steinitz became the first widely accepted champion in 1886, any strong player who could raise the money for a match could challenge. {052-S02}

Champions wrote rules that suited themselves. Emanuel Lasker wanted a challenger to win by two points. Under FIDE, Varma argued, Mikhail Botvinnik gained from a cap on entrants per country, which limited the strong Soviets who could threaten him.

The Soviet state chose its own heroes, preferring the loyal Anatoly Karpov to the outspoken Garry Kasparov. And a century after Steinitz, one challenge cycle still collapsed because nobody could fund the match.

Behind the Soviet dominance lay a school. Children were taught chess as they were taught maths, and the best players, Varma said, read patterns rather than calculating further ahead. Vishy Anand had none of that training, learned on the fly, and beat the world’s best in his teens.
## Machines and mammals

When engines overtook humans, many expected them to flatten chess into one computer style. The opposite happened, Varma said. The flattening had been done by the Soviet school; engines supplied concrete exceptions to its principles, and players developed styles of their own. {052-C04}

AlphaZero, which taught itself in a day, showed that humans had overvalued material against initiative. Yet the game is far from solved, and teenagers now sharpen their pattern recognition by playing huge volumes of games online.
## Chess and the nation

Shah then asked what chess says about a country. Not much, he said at first: the USSR ruled the game from Botvinnik to Kasparov and still collapsed. India’s rise impressed him more because the state did nothing to make it.
He tested a deliberately extreme theory, that talent is fixed at conception, so that a country’s grandmasters should simply track its population. {052-C10}

It fails. India has about 84 grandmasters for some 1,440 million people, Shah said, the United States 101 and Russia 236, while Bangladesh and Pakistan, both very large, have had little success in chess.

Nurture and community must do the rest: a family with money to spare for what Shah called “the silliness”, an early start, and parents who will travel to tournaments rather than push the child towards the JEE.
Varma added that excellence comes in clusters, often seeded by accident, and that India as a whole is the wrong unit.

Shah’s caution was about ambition. Chess needs a richer culture than cricket, he said, but leadership, innovation and literature need far more. “Just because you’ve got 84 heroes who are grandmasters, it doesn’t take you to 84 poets.” {052-C14}
At the very end, the two of them sat down to play a game.

second.label: Computer chess
second.head: All brain, no machine
second.deck: In 1948 Alan Turing designed a chess program that no computer could run
body: In 1948, Amit Varma said, Alan Turing and David Champernowne created a chess program called Turochamp. It was an algorithm on paper, and no computer then, or for some time after, was powerful enough to run it. {052-S09}

So it could never be tested. Turing died “too young and too tragically”, in Varma’s words, and Champernowne abandoned the project. Only after Moore’s Law kicked in did processing power catch up with such ideas.

Progress, when it came, was slow. Ken Thompson, another of Ajay Shah’s heroes, built Belle, the world computer champion in the early 1980s, which reached about 2,200 Elo. That, Varma admitted, is “stronger than me today”. {052-J12}

quote.text: So it is just an algorithm on paper that they have created, but they can never really test it.

second.caption: Turing’s paper engine

third.head: Taught in the nursery
body: Devangshu Datta, a friend of both hosts, played chess seriously in the 1980s. As a young player he would sweat through the opening and the middlegame against Soviet opponents, spend 40 minutes on a single move, and still lose. {052-S07}
Then, he told Amit Varma, the Soviet player would ask what he had been calculating. “It is taught to us in nursery that in this kind of formation you play like this.”
There was no internet and no database in those days, Varma said, so players from other countries had to work all of it out for themselves.
Ajay Shah’s favourite chess-book phrase captures the same gap. A deep insight, such as that the king is an attacking piece, would be prefaced with “as every Russian schoolboy knows”. {052-J09}
third.caption: Devangshu Datta’s Soviet lesson

p2.title: Moves and motives
p2.deck: From Steinitz in 1886 to grandmasters and poets: the episode’s argument, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The championship
sections.head: Whoever pays, plays
sections.caption: the history of the world title
body: Chess in the 19th century was unorganised, Amit Varma said. Wilhelm Steinitz became the first champion widely accepted by the community when he beat Johannes Zukertort in 1886. Zukertort had finished three points ahead of him at a great tournament in London in 1883.

There was no governing body, so the rule became that any strong challenger who could raise the money got a match. {052-S02} Siegbert Tarrasch had slightly better results but could not; Emanuel Lasker could, and kept the title for 27 years. {#lasker}

When José Raúl Capablanca came calling, Lasker demanded that the challenger win by two points, or the match would count as a draw and Lasker would keep the crown. Varma called it ridiculous, and “a precursor to future rules which are as ridiculous”.
## The rule-makers

After Alekhine died in 1945, FIDE took over. Its cycle capped how many players any one country could send, which looked fair, since the Soviets held most of the top spots. But Mikhail Botvinnik, Varma said, was close to the rule-makers, and fewer Soviet entrants meant fewer compatriots to threaten him. {052-S03} A drawn match let the champion keep his title; a deposed one got a rematch.
~ The state later picked its own favourite in Anatoly Karpov, “a party man”. In the 1990s, Garry Kasparov broke with FIDE over money for a match, asking where its legitimacy came from. {052-S06}

quote.text: whichever strong player wishes to challenge me, if they can come up with the funding for the game, I’ll play.

sections.label: The ideas
sections.head: Schoolboys and black boxes
sections.caption: how chess ideas evolved
body: Beginners think tactically, Amit Varma said: if I do this, he will do that. Deeper players think strategically, and much of that foundational thinking is credited to Wilhelm Steinitz.

The Soviet school built a pedagogy on it. Varma cited Adriaan de Groot’s study, which he dated to 1942: the best players do not think more moves ahead than amateurs, they are much better at pattern recognition. {052-C01} The Soviets formalised those patterns and taught them from childhood.
## Machines that diversified

Computers, many feared, would flatten chess, with everyone playing the same moves. The opposite happened. The flattening, Varma argued, had been done by the Soviet school; engines offered concrete exceptions to its principles, and players began to develop styles of their own. {052-C04}
Then came AlphaZero, given no human heuristics. Learning by playing itself, it showed, in Varma’s words, “that we were overvaluing material in contrast to initiative”. {052-C05}

~ Ajay Shah drew out the change in compensation. A 19th-century sacrifice was a precise combination repaid within a few moves; AlphaZero gives up material for position and waits ten or fifteen moves for a structural payoff.

quote.text: The opposite happens because a great flattening sound was the Soviet school of chess.

sections.label: Man and machine
sections.head: Bad moves, good bets
sections.caption: why chess is still a human game
body: Ajay Shah put a friend’s verdict to Amit Varma: was chess over? Varma answered with an analogy. If bots could perfectly imitate the two of them, would Shah stop talking to him? {052-C06}
Nor is the game solved. Endgame tablebases give perfect answers only with seven or fewer pieces on the board, engines tackle positions differently, and there is no single line that draws every game.
## Wrong on purpose

At the top, Varma said, the edge comes from deviating. A move that is suboptimal against perfect computer play may be excellent against a human, whose preparation does not cover it and who must start thinking, and second-guessing, at the board. {052-C07}

For a world championship match, the preparation runs to months. Each player works with a team of seconds whose names are kept secret, because “you profile the seconds and you can figure shit out”. {052-S12}

~ Magnus Carlsen tired of it all. Rather than give up six months to dreary study, he walked away from the title, telling the chess world to find another way. {052-S13} He now plays more rapid, blitz and Chess960, also known as Fischer Random.

quote.text: Will you stop talking to me, Ajay? You won’t, right? The human connection matters.

sections.label: The new generation
sections.head: Play more, panic less
sections.caption: chess as a spectator sport
body: Chess has become a spectator sport, Amit Varma said, and commentary is part of the reason. Commentators use engines to show the best moves, and grandmasters explain what the players are thinking. Ajay Shah was taken with events that show the audience both players’ heart rates. “I think that’s genius,” he said. {052-C09}

Varma saw a parallel with poker, which youth took over once players online could play in thirty months the hands Doyle Brunson took thirty years to play. Young chess players now put in the same volume, sharpening their pattern recognition. {052-C08}
## The calm one

Before the Candidates, Varma saw D Gukesh as high-variance, a player who could win or finish near the bottom. He admits he was partly wrong. Gukesh was never outplayed and lost only once, to Firouzja, after a blunder in time trouble.
One explanation, Varma said, is that until he became a grandmaster Gukesh did not use computers. He studied through humans and books, and is super solid on principles. {052-S16}
~ His coach, Grzegorz Gajewski, once Vishy Anand’s second, marvels at how calm he is. Varma has high hopes, though he feels Magnus Carlsen’s abdication has devalued the title.

quote.text: I just need to take you out of your prep somehow. And then we’ll play and I’ll outplay you, boss.

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Turning the knobs
sections.caption: what chess says about a nation
body: Ajay Shah asked what India’s chess boom says about India. His first answer was “a trivial debating point”. The USSR dominated chess from Botvinnik to Kasparov and collapsed anyway. It was a failed country, he said, and if Russia is good at one thing, it is “exporting all its talent”. {052-J04}

Even so, Shah respects India’s rise more than the Soviet one. The Soviet state filtered millions of children with heavy incentives, a project in which, as he put it, “some hormones were injected and some creature was produced”. {052-J05} India’s grandmasters bubbled up from families while the state did nothing.
## The filters
Shah then tested a theory that ability is fixed at conception, so that grandmasters should track population. The data reject it. {052-C10}

What else counts? The hosts’ friend Ayush reckons a family needs about $5,000 a head to afford what Shah called “the silliness”. {#ayush} The child must start before ten, with a computer, the internet and coaching, and parents must be able to travel to tournaments.

~ Amit Varma, quoting Steven Pinker, said nature gives you knobs and nurture turns them. {052-C11} India’s 1.4 billion, he argued, is a misleading number: perhaps only 10 to 20 million people live where children get leisure time that is not goal-directed.

quote.text: So you have one clear counter example where extreme success in chess went along with extreme and comprehensive societal and state failure.

sections.label: Chess and India
sections.head: Grandmasters aren’t poets
sections.caption: clusters, poets and lunchrooms
body: Does having 84 grandmasters mean India can have 84 poets? Not so fast, Ajay Shah said. {052-C14}

He laid out a spectrum. Cricket and the IPL need a simpler package of skills; chess needs somewhat more culture and community; leadership, innovation and literature need far more. India’s services exports, he said, mostly fill narrow roles in which a global firm supplies the culture and the strategy, and the worker can “shut up and turn the wrench”. Few Indian organisations work as talent factories, as he considers NIPFP and XKDR Forum to be.
## Accidents and clusters
Amit Varma was uneasy with India as the unit. You could look at Mylapur, he said, and call it an OECD country. {052-C13}

Excellence comes in clusters, he argued, often seeded by accident: Anand’s childhood in the Philippines helped make Tamil Nadu a chess hub. Shah agreed, and predicted many little cultures, of physicists and, at Varma’s prompting, podcasters, each of which could explode.
~ Shah’s test of such a culture is the lunchroom. Where work is just a job, people discuss Bollywood. As capability grows, ideas take over the lunch table. {052-C15}

quote.text: Little people talk about people, medium people talk about news, great minds talk about ideas.

side.boxTitle: The boy who solved too much
side.boxText: India’s first grandmaster learned without the Soviet machine. As a boy in the Philippines, Amit Varma said, Vishy Anand kept cracking a TV chess programme’s puzzle of the week, until it told him to stop entering. {052-S17}

contQuote.text: We are mammals. And we are subject to the foibles of mammals, which includes being able to read subtle muscle tone of each other’s faces, which never happens on a video call.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Rebels, prodigies, machines and wrestlers: the episode’s stories, and what they teach

stories.start: And Bobby Fisher is like a rebel in the system
stories.end: grows his big beard and the m you know, kind of leaves chess forever
stories.caption: Bobby Fischer’s rise and exit
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the rebel who took the crown and vanished
stories.head: Six-nil, then silence
body: As a teenager, Amit Varma said, Bobby Fischer did not do all that well in the interzonals. Soviet players such as Keres, Geller and Tal were really strong. {052-S04}
But he got better. Varma calls him a prodigal talent and “one of the true geniuses of the sport”, and a rebel in the system.
The rebel showed itself when Fischer decided not to play, and so did not qualify from the zonals. Then, Varma said, he decided he wanted to play after all.
One by one, the top three American qualifiers dropped out to make room for him. {#dropout} “And all three of them have to drop off for him to take the place, and he does,” Varma said.

He won a candidates match 6-0 against Taimanov. {#sixnil} He won another 6-0, destroyed the former champion Tigran Petrosian and, after forfeiting the first game of a famous match in Reykjavik, beat Boris Spassky for the title. “And you’re like wow,” Varma said.

The Soviet school then produced Anatoly Karpov, who qualified to challenge him in 1975. Fischer began setting bizarre conditions, Varma said, very like those Lasker had once set for Capablanca, such as a two-game gap. Essentially, he did not want to play.
~ He disappeared from chess, grew a big beard and became a recluse, and Karpov took over. “Now we can speculate about why that is,” Varma said. “But he’s reached the highest level he could have.”
stories.why: Even a lone genius needed three compatriots to step aside before he could climb. At the summit, he reached for the self-serving terms an earlier champion had used, and walked away rather than defend the crown.

stories.start: And I want to use this to put Anand's achievement in context
stories.end: It was a big deal to have any one of them
stories.caption: Anand’s Maruti 800
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on India’s first grandmaster
stories.head: Small car, big race
body: Vishy Anand, Amit Varma said, had none of the Soviet training. He had brilliant tactical sense and learned the rest on the fly. Winning the world championship that way was “like someone taking a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and winning”. {052-S08}

Behind the image of a nice, conventional gentleman, Varma said, Anand was an aggressive, ferocious player. Then he caught his tense. “And is, in fact,” he added. “I apologize, Vishy, if you’re watching this.” {052-J02}

When Varma was a teenager there was a race to become India’s first grandmaster. Pravin Thipsay earned norms but got stuck, and Dibyendu Barua had famously beaten Korchnoi at twelve. The younger Anand got there first.
~ “I remember the days we had zero,” Varma said. India now has 84. {#zero}
stories.why: Anand’s greatness, Varma suggested, is best measured against the infrastructure he never had. Having made it without the system, he became the hero a whole generation of Indian players grew up wanting to be.

stories.start: Now, what happens a few years ago is revolutionary, and this is Alpha Zero.
stories.end: applying the principles and heuristics it has discovered on its own by playing itself
stories.caption: AlphaZero’s day of self-play
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the machine that taught itself chess
stories.head: Centuries of chess in a day
body: AlphaZero, inspired by AlphaGo, was given no human principles or heuristics, Amit Varma said. It simply played chess against itself for 24 hours. {052-S10}

In that time it retraced the game’s history. It was taken with the French Defence, then decided it was a little inferior, much as humans did. It discovered the Berlin Defence, which Kramnik revived to beat Kasparov in the early 2000s.
Then it went beyond. In a match against Stockfish, then the strongest brute-force engine, it calculated a tenth or a hundredth as much, and still destroyed it. {#tenth}
~ What it had learned stayed in a black box, Varma said. Nobody knows what principles it discovered for itself; we know only that they work.
stories.why: Centuries of human wisdom were rediscovered, then surpassed, in a single day. Principles held for generations can be sound and still wrongly weighted: humans, the machine showed, had been overvaluing material against initiative. {052-C05}

stories.start: Like Haryana has a lot of women wrestlers
stories.end: So an accident of history created a cluster
stories.caption: Haryana’s women wrestlers
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how an accident made a cluster
stories.head: Wrestling with an accident
body: Haryana, Amit Varma said, is known to be very bad for its women in most ways. Yet it has a lot of women wrestlers. {052-C13}
It goes back to the late 1970s and a wrestler called Chandgi Ram. Wrestlers trained their sons to follow them, but he had no son, only a daughter, Sonika Kaliraman.

Then, in an accident of history, the Olympics opened up women’s wrestling. {#olympics} His eyes lit up, Varma said, and he trained his girl. His assistant, Mahavir Singh Phogat, trained his own three daughters, whose story became the film *Dangal*. “So an accident of history created a cluster,” Varma said. {052-S19}
~ India’s chess boom, he argued, is likewise one little cluster within India, not India itself.
stories.why: Clusters of excellence often begin when one person’s circumstance meets a change in the rules, Varma argued, rather than with any regional virtue. That is why he prefers the cluster to the country as the unit.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma stop playing serious chess at nineteen, in the early 1990s?
quiz.a: He realised he couldn’t be an Anand, and only Anand’s level paid a living.

quiz.q: Before FIDE, what did a challenger need in order to play the world champion?
quiz.a: The funding: any strong player who could raise the money got a match.

quiz.q: What did Adriaan de Groot’s study find about how the best players think?
quiz.a: They don’t calculate further ahead; they are far better at pattern recognition.

quiz.q: How long did AlphaZero play against itself before it relived all of chess history?
quiz.a: Twenty-four hours, rediscovering the French and Berlin Defences along the way.

quiz.q: Which wrestler, wanting a son to train, started Haryana’s cluster of women wrestlers?
quiz.a: Chandgi Ram, who trained his daughter when the Olympics opened up women’s wrestling.

quiz.q: What is Ajay Shah’s test of an organisation’s intellectual health?
quiz.a: Overhear its lunch conversations: Bollywood means just a job, ideas mean passion.
